chapter: Opening and the working musician's life
title: Playing with local rhythm sections; lessons from Sonny Stitt
summary: Handling unknown bands abroad with common standards, and learning consistency from Sonny Stitt.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: When you’re in Spain, you get with this local band, and you have a repertoire of tunes that you know, and that you hope that they know, do you get a little talk-through rehearsal with them beforehand? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Sometimes yes, sometimes no. I’ve had to just go right to the job and we have got five minutes. And you really learn how to quickly make decisions. For example there’s common tunes that everybody should know. And if they don’t know those tunes, you’re really in trouble. Like “I Got Rhythm” changes, certain blues, things like that, standards that are really considered across the board standards, like “Lady Be Good.” So if you don’t know these guys you first try a song like that and see how they are. Then you might try throwing some music at them and see if they can read. But those kind of jobs you’re kind of learning as you go. But I usually travel with a book of my things and some easier things that they could play if it’s not a great band, and I’ll try to meet them halfway. I mean obviously I love to work with my own band and I try to do that as much as I can, but a lot of times they just don’t have the kind of money to bring everybody over.
So being able to deal with those kind of situations is almost as important as the kind of player you are, because even if you’re a great player, you have to have the ability to be flexible.

You do. And you have to have the ability to not let things phase you that easily. I really learned from a master of that kind of thing, Sonny Stitt, the great saxophone player. I studied with him, I used to watch him play all the time. He did that his whole life. He just traveled around and played with local rhythm sections. And he learned to have a certain consistency in his playing no matter what else was going on behind him. And there’s a talent to that. It teaches you a discipline as a musician. If you can find guys that you’re really sympathetic with on the bandstand, or women, and you can hook up with them, that’s great. But you also have to learn to block out the bad influences and sometimes you’re literally just playing for yourself. And then even after the end of what seemed like a not-so-good night, you can at least say that you played good or you did the best you could. And then maybe the audience can hear a little bit of that.
